draft.title: Aggregate demand
card: Aggregate demand (AD) is the total spending on an economy's goods and services over a period. AD = C + I + G + (X - M).
C is household consumption, I is business investment, G is government spending, and X - M is exports less imports.
Higher consumer and business confidence can lift spending and so raise AD. Lower confidence can reduce it.
Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, which can raise consumption and investment. Higher incomes can raise consumption. Changes in these can shift AD.
draft.remember: AD is all spending in the economy, and confidence, interest rates and income can shift it.

a.q: Which of these is part of the investment (I) component of AD?
opts: A bakery in Ballarat buys a new oven
A family in Geelong buys a new sofa
The Victorian Government pays hospital nurses
A Melbourne shop sells jackets to a buyer in Japan
a.why: Investment is spending by businesses on capital goods such as machinery, and an oven is one. The sofa is consumption, which is tempting because it is also a purchase, but households buy it.
a.clue: Who is doing the buying, and is it a business?

b.q: The Reserve Bank lowers interest rates. Households in Bendigo borrow more and spend more on cars and renovations. What is the likely effect on AD?
opts: AD rises because consumption rises
AD falls because borrowing rises
AD stays the same because spending only moves
AD rises only if imports also rise
b.why: Cheaper borrowing can lift household spending, which raises the consumption part of AD. The idea that AD falls because borrowing rises is tempting but wrong, since borrowed money is spent on goods and services.
b.clue: Which part of C + I + G + (X - M) is changing?

a.best: A bakery in Ballarat buys a new oven

problems.detail: The clue 'Who is doing the buying, and is it a business?' nearly gives the answer away. The bakery is the only option where a business is buying, so a student can pick it without knowing what investment means.

In Australian national accounts, household spending on renovations (alterations and additions to dwellings) counts as private dwelling investment, not consumption. The answer still holds because of the car purchases, but 'renovations' muddies the C vs I distinction. Use another consumption item, such as holidays or furniture.

check.summary: Both questions have one clearly correct answer. The clue in (a) nearly hands over the answer, and household renovations in (b) are technically counted as investment rather than consumption, so that example should be swapped.

proposal.title: Aggregate demand
card: Aggregate demand (AD) is the total spending on an economy's goods and services over a period. AD = C + I + G + (X - M).
C is consumption: household spending on goods and services, such as food and furniture. I is investment: business spending on capital goods, such as machinery and buildings.
G is government spending, such as paying nurses and building roads. X - M is spending on our exports by other countries, less our spending on imports.
Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper, so they can lift C and I. Higher confidence and higher incomes can also raise spending. The reverse of each can lower AD.
proposal.remember: Add up C, I, G and X - M to get AD. Confidence, interest rates and income can shift it.

b.clue: Who is doing the extra spending?
